overview.text: Crop rotation is the planned sequence of different crops grown on the same field over time. Instead of repeatedly planting one crop, farmers choose a sequence suited to their crops and local conditions. Changing crops can interrupt the spread of pests, diseases, and weeds that thrive when a preferred host is repeatedly available. Different crops also explore soil at different depths, helping use nutrients and water from varied layers. Including legumes such as peas or clover can add nitrogen to the farming system and benefit crops that follow. Rotation is one way to manage soil nutrients and support soil health, though the best sequence depends on the farm.

key_facts.text: A rotation is defined by the order of crops planted on the same field; it may extend across multiple seasons or years.
Changing crops can reduce pest, disease, and weed pressure, but pests that move widely may be harder to control through rotation alone.
Some legumes support nitrogen fixation, and legumes in a rotation can provide nitrogen for a following crop.
Crops with different rooting depths can draw on different soil layers; rotations can also help distribute water and nutrients through the soil profile.
Rotation plans should account for the crops and local conditions: the previous crop can affect later disease risks, soil fertility, and soil structure.
